title: Ninja Crispi Review Roundup: India's Viral Glass Air Fryer Cooks in the Open, at a Premium
excerpt: The 1700W PowerPod-and-glass system wins Indian reviewers on visibility and cleanup, but fixed temperatures, hot heavy containers and a Rs 19,990 list price are the trade-offs.
body:
• The Ninja Crispi FN101IN (Rs 19,990 list; seen at Rs 14,999 in festive sales) replaces the pull-out basket with two glass containers — 1.4-litre and 3.8-litre — under a detachable 1700W PowerPod heater.
  • Reviewers in India praise exactly what the glass promises: you can watch food cook without opening anything, the containers double as serving and storage dishes, and cleanup is easy. The Hindu's testers took it from marinades to reheated leftovers.
  • The consistent criticism is control: the four functions (air fry, roast, recrisp, keep warm) run at fixed temperatures with no manual temperature adjustment, which Digit calls a significant restriction at this price.
  • Glass containers get hot and the large one is heavy when full — this is a premium two-to-four-person appliance, not a big-family batch cooker.

Every air fryer asks you to cook blind. The Ninja Crispi — the glass air fryer that has been all over Indian social feeds this festive season — removes the drawer entirely: food cooks in a transparent glass container under a detachable heating unit Ninja calls the PowerPod, so you can see the browning happen. The Hindu's reviewers spent a festive week with the Indian model, cooking from marinades to leftover-reheating; reviews from Digit and Gizbot, who tested the same FN101IN unit, fill in where the viral clips stop.

What it is

The India variant pairs a 1700W PowerPod with two CleanCrisp borosilicate glass containers, 1.4 litres and 3.8 litres, with crisper plates and storage lids. There are four functions — air fry, roast, recrisp and keep warm — and the containers are rated microwave-, freezer- and dishwasher-safe, so the same vessel can marinate, cook, serve and store. It carries a two-year warranty, with Indian support handled through a local partner, according to Digit's review.

How it cooked

Over about a week of cooking, Digit's test unit produced satisfying potato crispers and chicken and reheated leftovers successfully, and proved straightforward to clean — the glass, the reviewers found, is the strongest part of the design. Gizbot, testing the same Air Fry, Roast and Recrisp functions, likewise rated visibility, versatile containers and convenient reheating as the appliance's real advantages over a conventional basket fryer — useful in Indian kitchens, where the recrisp function meets a daily reality of rotis, pakoras and last night's tikkas.

The catch: fixed temperatures

Every reviewer lands on the same reservation. Each function runs at a fixed temperature, the operating temperatures are not clearly communicated, and there is no dial to set 180°C because a recipe says so. "At Rs 19,999, time-only control feels restrictive," Digit concludes, calling the missing temperature adjustment the design's one significant flaw. Handling is the second caveat: the glass containers come out hot — mitts are not optional — and the 3.8-litre container is heavy when filled. Capacity suits small households; large families batch-cooking for a Diwali party will feel the ceiling.

Price and verdict

The list price is Rs 19,990-19,999 depending on the listing; festive-season selling prices have been far lower — Gizbot recorded Rs 14,999 during the sale period, and Flipkart listings showed the same Rs 14,999 against a Rs 19,990 MRP. The verdict across reviews is consistent: the Crispi earns its premium if you value visibility, serve-from-the-container convenience and easy cleaning — and if your cooking rarely demands precise temperatures. Bakers and recipe-followers who cook by degrees should look at a conventional model with full controls, or wait for a Crispi that has them. See Gizbot's full review for its mode-by-mode testing.
